{"id": "26:84/q07", "question": "Is it permissible or desirable to pray for righteous praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q07/p1", "position": "Yes, when sought for God's pleasure and grounded in good deeds.", "reasons": "Malik says one may wish to be seen among doers of good if intending God's pleasure; Ibn al-ʿArabi transmits his restriction to a good reputation among the righteous. Al-Jishumi approves prayer for descendants and honorable later repute. Al-Bursawi ties genuine remembrance to deeds, character, and speech; al-Alusi says the prayer implicitly asks for success in good works."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q08", "question": "How was this prayer answered or evidenced?", "turns_on": "The notes cite broad public praise, prophetic descendants and scriptures, and recurring liturgical blessings as forms of fulfillment.", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q08/p1", "position": "Abraham receives lasting praise and acceptance among religious communities.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, and others say people of every religion praise or love him; al-Tabari's Ikrima calls it worldly good or reward and cites 29:27 and 16:122. Ibn ʿAbbas cites 37:108. Kuran Yolu says Muslims, Jews, and Christians honor him, and Muslim prayers name Abraham with Muhammad. Study Quran points to 19:50; Kuran Yolu reports proofs that all Abraham's requests except the one for his father were granted."}, {"id": "26:84/q08/p2", "position": "His descendants include prophets, especially Muhammad, who renew his remembrance and religion.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi cites Abraham's prophetic descendants and the prayer formula blessing Muhammad as Abraham was blessed; Ibn ʿAshur says later scriptures preserve Abraham's name. Islahi says Israelite prophets and Muhammad made his message endure and spread. Kuran Yolu adds the command to follow Abraham's religion, citing 16:123, 3:95, and 4:125; Study Quran attributes fulfillment in Muhammad to Q and R."}, {"id": "26:84/q08/p3", "position": "Blessings on Muhammad include blessings on Abraham in prayers and sermons.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi points to prayers and pulpits; al-Biqaʿi and Kuran Yolu cite the blessing formula naming both prophets."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q09", "question": "What merit is reported for reciting Abraham's prayer after ablution?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q09/p1", "position": "A report promises guidance, provision, healing, forgiveness, truthful renown, martyrdom, and Paradise benefits to one reciting it before obligatory prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits the Prophetic report promising Paradise food, drink and homes, expiation, blessed life, wisdom, and other benefits; al-Hasan adds a prayer for parents."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q10", "question": "How does Abraham's request fit the sequence of his prayers and the surrounding narrative?", "turns_on": "These notes address different links: the prayer sequence, Abraham's life setting, and the sura's narrative arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q10/p1", "position": "It follows requests for wisdom and righteousness and seeks a lasting, spiritual perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reads knowledge first, then inward virtue and lasting honor rather than outward appearance or wealth. Al-Tabatabai says essential righteousness completes the gift of wisdom and cites 16:122; Ibn ʿAshur says the earlier 'righteous' request sums up prophets, martyrs, and the righteous."}, {"id": "26:84/q10/p2", "position": "The prayer accompanies Abraham's break with his people and migration.", "reasons": "Islahi locates it at the sensitive point of declaring acquittal and migrating."}, {"id": "26:84/q10/p3", "position": "The Abraham narrative advances the sura's preaching pattern and bridges the interval between Noah and Moses.", "reasons": "Islahi says it shares the preceding anecdote's purpose and recurring closing verses, and fills the prior sura's gap because Abraham was the most prominent messenger between Noah and Moses."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q11", "question": "How does this request connect to other Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "The links differ by parallel: fulfillment in remembrance verses, the later messenger prayer, or divinely granted love.", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q11/p1", "position": "Other verses speak of Abraham's enduring good remembrance and worldly good.", "reasons": "Yahya points to 37:78; Ibn ʿAbbas via al-Razi to 37:108; Ibn Kathir to 37:108–110; Mujahid to 29:27 and 16:122; al-Tabatabai to 37:108 and 19:50, and Study Quran to 19:50."}, {"id": "26:84/q11/p2", "position": "The prayer resembles the request for a later messenger and community in 2:128–129.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi cites 2:129 and the hadith 'I am Abraham's prayer' for the final community and Muhammad; al-Tabatabai reports 2:128–129 and that hadith but calls its equation with this verse unclear."}, {"id": "26:84/q11/p3", "position": "God's placing love for Moses and believers among people illuminates Abraham's request.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites 20:39 and 19:96; Ibn ʿAshur also connects Moses' divinely given love in 20:39 with Abraham's desired remembrance and notes the earlier family prayer in 25:74."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q12", "question": "What does the adjacent request for wisdom and inclusion among the righteous mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q12/p1", "position": "It asks for essential righteousness completing wisdom and full readiness for divine mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib contrasts ṣalāḥ with corruption as preservation of original nature and its proper effects. Al-Tabatabai says soundness of essence, beyond deeds alone, leaves no corrupt belief or action obstructing mercy; he cites 7:58 and 16:122. Ibn ʿAshur says 'the righteous' includes prophets and messengers, with the broad category placed last as a summation, and reads the petition as seeking ranks including Noah, Hud, Salih, martyrs, and the righteous."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q13", "question": "What does Abraham's wider speech teach about religious reasoning and worship?", "turns_on": "The notes draw distinct lessons about proof, the object of worship, and the order of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q13/p1", "position": "Truth in religion is established by proof, and imitation is condemned.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi explicitly affirms religious argument and criticizes imitation in the surrounding passage."}, {"id": "26:84/q13/p2", "position": "Worship belongs to the one who originates basic blessings and controls benefit and harm.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi draws this criterion from Abraham's argument."}, {"id": "26:84/q13/p3", "position": "Supplication should begin with monotheism, following the prophets' method.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi derives this order from Abraham's speech and prayer."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q14", "question": "How does the wider speech explain provision and healing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q14/p1", "position": "God creates provision and cure, while medicine and other natural factors are causes within habits He establishes.", "reasons": "Against natural philosophers, al-Jishumi compares medicine with parents and food: God creates offspring, satiety, and quenching. Natural causes would yield uniform immediate effects, but nature does not reason and drugs have no known feature that itself heals. God made some things nourish, poison, or heal and could have established opposite habits."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q15", "question": "Why did Abraham pray for his father in the following verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q15/p1", "position": "He relied on a promise or rational obligation until the prayer was forbidden.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi gives these alternatives concerning 26:86; Kuran Yolu notes that exegetes except the father prayer from the requests granted."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q16", "question": "What inward reading is given to this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q16/p1", "position": "The prophets symbolize spirit or heart, while their peoples' denial symbolizes the soul resisting discipline and perfected morals.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani extends this allegory across the chapter: fearing God is avoiding vices; a trustworthy messenger conveys certain received truths without illusion or fantasy."}]}
{"id": "26:84/q17", "question": "Why does Ibn Qutayba cite this prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:84/q17/p1", "position": "It exemplifies a truthful legacy while he argues for scholarly investigation of hidden meanings in transmitted language.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba discusses proverbs, idioms, and reports that need inquiry to uncover their meanings."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q01", "question": "Which earlier day does يَوْمَ specify, and how is it parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q01/p1", "position": "It is an appositional substitute for the earlier day when people are raised.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī identify 26:87 as the antecedent; al-Ālūsī says the repetition magnifies the day's terror and prepares for 26:89. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn stress that an apposition shares its governing verb with its antecedent, a constraint relevant to the dispute over the speaker."}]}

{"id": "26:88/q03", "question": "What is the inward sense of this day?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q03/p1", "position": "It is the approach to the divine presence for acceptance of God's grace.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports this reading from Baḥr."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q04", "question": "What object of يَنفَعُ is understood?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q04/p1", "position": "The object is omitted because it is understood: wealth and children benefit no one.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī supplies the understood person as the object; al-Ṭabrisī likewise presupposes an omitted object when discussing the following exception."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q05", "question": "How can the following exception be parsed with يَنفَعُ?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative clause substitutes for the understood object or is parsed as an exception.", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q05/p1", "position": "The following relative clause is accusative as a substitute for the omitted object of 'benefit'.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī explains the resulting sense as no person being benefited by wealth or children except the person who comes to God."}, {"id": "26:88/q05/p2", "position": "The following relative clause is accusative as an exception.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī offers this as the alternative syntactic analysis."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q06", "question": "What sort of benefit do wealth and children fail to give on that day?", "turns_on": "Whether the denial includes good works and righteous children without qualification, or leaves a benefit for Muslims whose deeds and children are righteous.", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q06/p1", "position": "They cannot secure, ransom, defend, or otherwise help a person at Resurrection.", "reasons": "Muqātil says neither averts punishment after death. Al-Ṭabrisī says wealth cannot ransom its owner from hardship and children cannot bear a parent's sins; Abū Ḥayyān contrasts their worldly power to ransom and defend. Ibn Kathīr says even earth-filling gold or all people offered as ransom would fail. Al-Biqāʿī adds that wealth cannot purchase an intercessor or powerful defender, sons cannot support or console, and lesser things are still less useful. Bursevī extends the denial even to wealth spent on good works and righteous sons capable of intercession. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains that worldly social bonds and assigned causal power are conventional and severed when Resurrection discloses reality (6:94; 23:101; 37:25–26); this extends to learning, craft, and beauty. The Study Quran cites the recurring theme in 3:10, 3:116, 9:55, 31:33, 34:35–37, 58:17, 60:3, and 64:15. The Prophet's answer about Ibn Judʿān says his hospitality and kin care will not benefit him because he did not seek forgiveness for his sin on Judgment Day."}, {"id": "26:88/q06/p2", "position": "Believers can benefit from good deeds and righteous children, though disbelievers' wealth and children cannot help without sound hearts.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports al-Layth: disbelievers boasted of wealth and children, while Muslims may benefit from their deeds and from a righteous child whether the child dies first or later prays for the parent. ʿAlī, as reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, contrasts wealth and children as the world's harvest with deeds as the afterlife's harvest, while allowing that God grants both to some people."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q07", "question": "Why is wealth called مَالٌ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q07/p1", "position": "It is so called because it draws people toward itself.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports this explanation from al-Tharī, using the sense of inclining."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q08", "question": "What does بَنُونَ designate here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is confined to actual sons or extends to all possible helpers.", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q08/p1", "position": "It means sons in its ordinary sense.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly gives the ordinary sense as his own explanation before mentioning a broader alternative."}, {"id": "26:88/q08/p2", "position": "It stands for helpers or supporters more generally.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this broad interpretation; al-Ālūsī reports it as another view. Al-Qurṭubī explains sons as supporters: if one's own son cannot help, nobody else can."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q09", "question": "What grammatical form is بَنُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q09/p1", "position": "It is appended to the sound masculine plural pattern and loses its nūn in an iḍāfa construction.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī gives بنو آدم and بني آدم as examples of the nūn's loss in construct forms."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q10", "question": "How is a name such as بَنُونَ shortened in vocative truncation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q10/p1", "position": "Only its final nūn is dropped, preserving a name of at least three letters.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says paired jointly added suffixes are removed together, as in مسلمان, but a name like بنون cannot be shortened below three letters; its remainder may count as an unaugmented name. He illustrates other vocative truncations with عثمان to عثم, مروان to مرو, and أسماء to أسم, citing matching poetry."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q11", "question": "Why are wealth and sons named as examples?", "turns_on": "Whether the choice emphasizes worldly adornments, the strongest human support, or the immediately preceding mention of Abraham's father.", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q11/p1", "position": "They are the chief adornments and sources of status, security, and comfort in worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verse negates worldly attachments and names their greatest adornments. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report the same wider sense of all worldly goods and attractions; Abū Ḥayyān cites 18:46. The Study Quran calls these sources of worldly status, security, and comfort. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī extends the examples to all conventionally valued means to material ends, including learning, craft, and beauty."}, {"id": "26:88/q11/p2", "position": "Sons are named because a son is the strongest likely supporter, so the failure of sons implies the failure of other helpers.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī draws that inference; al-Biqāʿī similarly says lesser means are even less useful after wealth and sons fail."}, {"id": "26:88/q11/p3", "position": "The mention of sons recalls Abraham's father: Abraham could not benefit him.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this explanation from an unnamed authority because Abraham's father was just mentioned; Iṣlāḥī likewise says Āzar's having Abraham as a son could not save him."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q12", "question": "How does the following sound-heart exception qualify this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q12/p1", "position": "A sound heart free of associationism matters where wealth and children fail.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām transmits Qatāda through Saʿīd defining the sound heart as free of associationism. Bursevī reports al-Layth that disbelievers' boasts of wealth and children cannot help without sound hearts; al-Ālūsī says this day's description prepares for the following exception in 26:89."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q13", "question": "What does Abraham's prayer and this day show about divine and family help?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q13/p1", "position": "People need God's support to face the terrors of Resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī infers this from Abraham's plea not to be disgraced: weak human constitution cannot face that day without divine aid."}, {"id": "26:88/q13/p2", "position": "Abraham's father could not be saved through his son, and the request concerning him was the exception to Abraham's granted prayers.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī uses Āzar as the case showing that a child cannot benefit a parent; Kur'an Yolu reports that exegetes offer various proofs that all Abraham's requests were granted except the one concerning his father."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q14", "question": "How is the Abraham account placed in the sūra's sequence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q14/p1", "position": "It serves the same preaching purpose as the preceding account and ends with the recurring verses.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī makes this comparison with the preceding anecdote."}, {"id": "26:88/q14/p2", "position": "It fills the gap after Noah in the previous sūra, since Abraham was the most prominent messenger between Noah and Moses.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī gives this placement within the sequence of prophetic accounts."}, {"id": "26:88/q14/p3", "position": "The sūra can be classed as a digression because its discourse returns afterward to prophets and earlier communities.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī reports this classification from some scholars."}]}
{"id": "26:88/q15", "question": "What narrative wording presents Resurrection as certain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:88/q15/p1", "position": "Past-tense verbs describe future Resurrection events to present them as certain.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān identifies أتى, أزلفت, and برزت after the rebuke of the idolaters."}]}

He says unabbikum writes a dammated hamza with wāw after alif, while other double or triple hamzas may use a single alif; hāʾulāʾ joins the alerting particle, omitting its alif, as in yā ayyuhā. {"id": "26:89/q01", "question": "What does the exception say benefits a person on that Day?", "turns_on": "Whether man is disconnected, an object or subject of yanfaʿ, or a figurative substitute for wealth and children; whether an omitted noun is required and whether the reading covers the poor and childless.", "positions": [{"id": "26:89/q01/p1", "position": "The exception is disconnected: wealth and children do not benefit, whereas a person arriving with a sound heart benefits from its soundness.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī calls it a separate statement. Abū Ḥayyān prefers the apparent syntax and denies that an omitted noun is needed; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise says it covers rich, poor, parents, and childless alike. The latter rejects connected readings for restricting benefit to wealthy parents and rejects an unnecessary ellipsis. The Shaykh in al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān in al-Ālūsī also deny the ellipsis. Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that disconnectedness alone leaves the grammatical difficulty unresolved."}, {"id": "26:89/q01/p2", "position": "The exception is disconnected but an implied 'state of soundness' supplies the item that benefits.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says a state must be supplied because soundness is not the same kind as wealth and children; al-Samīn defends this by comparing the impossible bare exception 'horses neigh except camels.' Al-Kashf says Abū Ḥayyān instead changes the antecedent from wealth to the whole sentence. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that this ellipsis is needless."}, {"id": "26:89/q01/p3", "position": "The exception is connected to the people benefited: only the person with a sound heart can benefit from wealth spent well and righteous children.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the heart directs spending in obedience and teaching children religion, while remaining free of their temptation. Al-Nasafī makes man the object of yanfaʿ; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report this free-object parse. Al-Samīn also allows an omitted general object or excluded person and cites a poetic line about escaping only with a sword sheath and loincloth. Ibn ʿĀshūr insists the person is benefited rather than benefactor, with an implied general benefactor and rhetorical abstraction: the heart causes its owner's benefit. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that this reading overlooks poor or childless people. Muqātil, Ibn Kathīr, Bursawī, and al-Biqāʿī connect benefit to faith and good use of possessions."}, {"id": "26:89/q01/p4", "position": "The exception is connected to wealth and children belonging to a sound-hearted person; their charity and righteous upbringing benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says one subject-substitute analysis lets children predominate over wealth, giving the righteous child who benefits self and others; another supplies a possessive before man. Abū al-Baqāʾ gives a subject-substitute analysis involving predominance and intercession, but al-Samīn says it conflates the two routes. Al-Ālūsī describes man as nominative with an implied noun. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the connected restriction to wealthy parents."}, {"id": "26:89/q01/p5", "position": "The exception treats worldly wealth and children as affluence, while the sound heart is the only enduring religious wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts worldly possessions and children with religious wealth; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī give the same figurative connection. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes the implied noun and figurative use of affluence, and rejects restricting the contrast to possessors of worldly riches. Thawbān reports the Prophet naming a remembering tongue, grateful heart, and righteous spouse the best wealth after the hoarding verse."}, {"id": "26:89/q01/p6", "position": "The connected exception substitutes the sound heart for wealth and children altogether.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī's illustration answers a question about Zayd's wealth and sons by affirming soundness of heart instead. Al-Zamakhsharī gives a state-based connected exception and a corresponding rhetorical illustration; al-Ālūsī repeats the Zayd example and also permits connection through an implied condition, illustrated by a greeting that is a painful blow."}]}
{"id": "26:89/q02", "question": "What nuance does أَتَى add to coming to God?", "turns_on": "Whether Arabic lexical usage and Qurʾānic examples support a special ease in atā.", "positions": [{"id": "26:89/q02/p1", "position": "Atā denotes an easy arrival, while jāʾa is broader and may describe more difficult arrivals.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib draws the distinction. Al-Sāmarrāʾī notes derivatives of atā for a well-traveled path and easy water channels, and cites strenuous Qurʾānic arrivals with jāʾa, including 23:27, 50:19, 18:71, 18:74, and 19:27, 88–90."}, {"id": "26:89/q02/p2", "position": "The lexicons generally treat atā and jāʾa as equivalents without this stated distinction.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī observes that lexicographers gloss each verb by the other."}]}
{"id": "26:89/q03", "question": "When does coming to God occur in the inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:89/q03/p1", "position": "It is arrival at a moment of watchfulness before God.", "reasons": "Baḥr relates this to the heart originally created as a mirror for divine attributes, later tarnished by attachment to the created world."}]}
{"id": "26:89/q04", "question": "What is the sound heart?", "turns_on": "Whether soundness names minimum saving faith, broader moral purification, detachment from creation, or a special inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "26:89/q04/p1", "position": "It is free of shirk, grounded in sincere monotheistic faith.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Zayd and others give this core gloss. Ibn Zayd expressly says no one is free of sins. Ibn ʿAbbās phrases it as testimony that there is no god but God; al-Muqātil says this makes wealth and offspring useful at resurrection. Ibn Kathīr adds sincere devotion. Ibn Sīrīn's reported concern about al-Ḥajjāj asks whether he would die with this monotheistic heart despite his sins. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the wording supports a general sense while freedom from shirk remains paramount."}, {"id": "26:89/q04/p2", "position": "It is free of shirk, doubt, disbelief, and hypocrisy, with certain and sincere faith.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī attributes the composite gloss to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, Muqātil, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan and most interpreters; he infers certainty and sincerity. Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid in al-Ṭabrisī include doubt. Al-Nasafī cites 2:10 for diseased unbelieving and hypocritical hearts. Al-Ālūsī says this transmitted sense best fits the context; faith is necessary for benefit from possessions.
